prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- Red Cross President and CEO Mark W. Everson has stepped down after revelations he was "engaged in a personal relationship with a subordinate employee," the organization announced Tuesday. Mark W. Everson says he is leaving his post, effective immediately, for "personal and family reasons." The Red Cross Board of Governors asked for and received Everson's  resignation after it "concluded that the situation reflected poor judgment on Mr. Everson's part and diminished his ability to lead the organization in the future,"  the Red Cross said in a statement on its Web site. Everson, 53, said in a written statement that he was leaving the $500,000-per-year job "for personal and family reasons, and deeply regret it is impossible for me to continue in a job so recently undertaken." Everson -- who is married and has two children -- joined the Red Cross as president and CEO last May. The organization became aware of Everson's relationship with a female Red Cross employee 10 days ago, Chief Public Affairs Officer Suzy C. DeFrancis told CNN in a telephone interview. "I think the board acted very quickly," she said, adding that the woman remains in her job. About Everson, DeFrancis said, "We're grateful for his service." The board of governors on Tuesday appointed Mary S. Elcano, general counsel and five-year Red Cross employee, as interim president and CEO. Everson had worked in the Bush administration from August 2001 -- including serving as commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service -- until he was hired by the Red Cross. "This is flabbergasting, that's all I can say. It's completely contrary to his public persona that he evidenced while he was at the IRS," said Suzanne Ross McDowell, a Washington-based attorney who served on an advisory committee to the IRS division that deals with tax-exempt organizations. "From the standpoint of exempt organizations on the non-profit sector, it's just another news story that we would rather not see," she said. "It's got nothing to do with the Red Cross," said Ira Milstein, a New York lawyer specializing in corporate governance who has worked with the organization and was impressed with Everson. "He was a team player and a good leader. To have him fall off a cliff like this is just sad." A search committee has been formed to begin the process of finding Everson's permanent replacement, the organization said. The job has been a challenging one. Marsha J. Evans resigned as president in 2005, after the Red Cross response to Hurricane Katrina came under fire. Four years earlier, Bernadine Healy quit the post after the organization was criticized for mishandling donations intended for victims of the September 11 terrorist attacks and collecting vast quantities of blood that was not needed and ultimately thrown out. Healy told reporters she "had no choice" about her resignation. Meanwhile, DeFrancis acknowledged Tuesday that, 14 years after a court ordered the agency to improve its collection of blood, it has yet to meet federal safety and quality-control requirements. **Mark W. Everson Steps Down as American Red Cross Chief After Personal Relationship With Employee**

**WASHINGTON —** Mark W. Everson has resigned as president and chief executive of the American Red Cross after the organization’s board concluded that he had engaged in a personal relationship with a subordinate employee, the charity announced.

The Red Cross said its Board of Governors accepted Everson’s resignation after learning of the relationship and determining that his actions showed “poor judgment” and had compromised his ability to lead the organization effectively. The organization said the matter did not involve questions about the stewardship of Red Cross funds or the delivery of disaster-relief services.

“The Board of Governors concluded that the situation reflected poor judgment on Mr. Everson’s part and diminished his ability to lead the organization in the future,” the American Red Cross said in a statement. The charity added that it remained focused on its humanitarian mission, including disaster response, blood collection and support for military families.

Everson, a former commissioner of the Internal Revenue Service and former deputy director of the Office of Management and Budget, had taken over the Red Cross earlier in the year. His departure came after only a brief tenure at the top of one of the nation’s best-known charitable organizations.

In its announcement, the Red Cross said it would move quickly to ensure continuity in operations and leadership. Senior officials emphasized that the organization’s nationwide network of volunteers, chapters and blood-service operations would continue functioning without interruption.

Everson’s resignation is the latest in a series of leadership disruptions at the American Red Cross, which has faced repeated scrutiny over management, governance and disaster response.

The organization’s leadership troubles drew national attention after the Sept. 11, 2001, terrorist attacks, when then-president Bernadine Healy clashed with the board over the handling of donations to the Liberty Fund, a special fund created for victims and families affected by the attacks. Critics questioned whether all donated money was being used as donors expected. Healy left the organization later that year amid tensions with the board.

Her successor, Marsha J. Evans, a former Navy rear admiral and leader of the Girl Scouts of the USA, was pushed out in 2005 following criticism of the Red Cross response to Hurricane Katrina. Although the organization played a central role in sheltering and assisting evacuees, it was faulted by lawmakers and watchdogs for coordination problems and uneven service delivery during one of the largest disasters in U.S. history.

The Red Cross later undertook governance reforms, including changes intended to clarify the roles of its board and management and strengthen oversight. Everson’s appointment had been viewed as part of an effort to stabilize the institution and restore public confidence.

Everson brought significant federal management experience to the position. As IRS commissioner, he led the tax agency during a period of modernization and enforcement initiatives. Before that, he held senior roles in the George W. Bush administration and had experience in both government and private-sector management.

The American Red Cross, chartered by Congress, is responsible for providing disaster relief, collecting and distributing much of the nation’s blood supply, offering health and safety training, and supporting members of the military and their families. Because of its prominent public role and reliance on donations, the organization has often faced close examination from Congress, regulators, donors and the public.

The board said it would begin the process of selecting a permanent successor while relying on interim leadership to maintain operations. Officials said the organization’s immediate priority was to reassure donors, volunteers and the communities it serves that its work would continue.

“This organization is larger than any one individual,” the Red Cross said, stressing that its mission remained unchanged. “The American Red Cross will continue to provide compassionate care and critical assistance to people in need.”

Its prominence has made its internal governance a matter of public interest, especially when failures or controversies emerge.
